title: Vimal Shah Carves a Marble Mountain

title_i18n.en: Vimal Shah Carves a Marble Mountain

subtitle: How a Jain Minister Raised a Marble Forest in the Arbuda Hills
moral: Patronage can turn wealth into beauty that outlives fear.

sources.citation: Vimal Vasahi consecration inscription, VS 1088 (1031-32 CE), Epigraphia Indica, vol. IX
Prithvipal's Hastishala inscription, 1147-49 CE, Dilwara, Epigraphia Indica series
sources.note: Evidence for later additions by Vimal Shah's descendants.

sources.citation: M.A. Dhaky, 'The Chronology of the Solanki Temples of Gujarat,' Journal of the Madhya Pradesh Itihas Parishad 3 (1961)
sources.note: Foundational technical dating of Solanki monuments.

panels.shot: sweeping low-angle wide of Vimal Shah before a gleaming marble mandapa rising from the misty Arbuda hills

dialogue.text: In Bhima I’s war-scarred age, Jain minister Vimal Shah dared to carve a mountain of marble, raising a shrine whose quiet outlasted a king’s fear.

panels.shot: slow push-in on Vimal Shah at a court balcony overlooking Anahilapataka

dialogue.text: It is the early eleventh century. From Anahilapataka, Chaulukya king Bhima I rules Gujarat; his Jain minister Vimal Shah counts coin, weighs risk…and watches the land steady itself after storms.

panels.shot: medium interior shot of a council chamber table with maps and ledgers

dialogue.text: The court’s records call him a minister and governor, not a prince. He is a Jain merchant risen by skill: steward of revenue, adviser of routes and roads, a man whose wealth moves silently.

panels.shot: wide shot of Gujarat landscape with distant shrine and caravan

dialogue.text: Gujarat’s shrines and markets rise again. Scholars later note: by 1031, the king’s treasury can spare patronage. Into this recovered breath, Vimal Shah decides to pour his own wealth.

panels.shot: intimate medium shot inside a Jain domestic shrine

dialogue.text: He is bound to the Jain path, devoted to Adinatha. In his household shrine, he bows with the same discipline he uses for ledgers, and a question hardens within him: what shall this fortune serve?

panels.shot: high-angle wide of Mount Abu’s rocky slopes at dawn

dialogue.text: He looks toward the Arbuda hills—Mount Abu, remote and cool above the plains. The choice is bold: not a city shrine, but a high refuge, where a temple to Adinatha will crown the rock.

panels.shot: bird’s-eye shot of a rocky plateau being surveyed

dialogue.text: We do not know the architects’ names; their plans are lost. But the inscription that survives will remember the patron: Vimal Shah, who marked out this stone, intent on raising a marble forest.

panels.shot: dynamic wide shot of quarry and caravan line

dialogue.text: White Makrana marble—hard, fine, luminous—is dragged across distances to this height. Panel by panel, scholars will later trace this stone’s grain and know: this was no village shrine.

panels.shot: low-angle interior wide of rising mandapa skeleton with scaffolding

dialogue.text: The core plan takes shape: a hall with rings of pillars, a sanctum for Adinatha, and a cloister of small shrines around. This cloister form will become the very image of western Indian Jain architecture.

panels.shot: close-up on Vimal Shah’s face watching an artisan carve

dialogue.speaker: vimal_shah
dialogue.text: Let no space be idle. Let stone remember every vow.

panels.shot: wide shot of the completed cloister courtyard

dialogue.text: Cloister shrines ring the courtyard, each precise, each echoing the next. Later historians will see in this plan a standard: a pattern that spreads from Arbuda to many Jain sites of the west.

panels.shot: medium shot of inscription being incised on stone

dialogue.text: In Vikrama Samvat 1088—1031 to 1032 CE by modern reckoning—the consecration inscription records it: this is Vimal Vasahi, Vimal’s temple, dedicated to Adinatha on Mount Abu’s Dilwara plateau.

panels.shot: interior wide of sanctum entrance with ceremony in progress

dialogue.text: The record speaks of consecration, not spectacle. No accounts of prabandha cost survive as ledgers; later stories exaggerate sums. The inscription simply fixes what matters: patron, deity, date, place.

panels.shot: low-angle interior shot of the carved ceiling looking upward

dialogue.text: Inside, the ceiling falls like a marble lotus, every ring bitten into with care. No blood, no battle is carved here. In an age of swords, this minister spent his strength on stillness.

panels.shot: time-lapse style wide of the temple exterior across decades

dialogue.text: Years turn. Bhima I’s court ebbs and flows, new rulers rise, but the Arbuda temple endures. Later, Vimal Shah’s own kin will add more—elephants, halls—leaving new inscriptions of their day.

panels.shot: medium shot of a later patron overseeing elephant sculptures in a courtyard

dialogue.text: A century on, Prithvipal’s Hastishala inscription, dated 1147–49 CE, speaks of the elephant court and later additions. The core shrine remains Vimal’s; the complex becomes a layered family legacy.

panels.shot: close-up of weathered inscription slabs set in a temple wall

dialogue.text: Centuries later, epigraphists lean close to these letters, copying them into Epigraphia Indica. Historians like M.A. Dhaky will sort dates and styles, fixing the temple in the chronology of Solanki monuments.

panels.shot: present-day interior wide of visitors walking softly through the hall

dialogue.text: Today, the cool marble still drinks the footsteps of pilgrims and visitors. The chaos of Bhima I’s time is gone; Vimal Shah’s decision remains, cut into stone, in every cloistered cell and pillar.

panels.shot: concluding slow pull-back from a contemplative Vimal Shah ghostlike amid the temple

dialogue.text: In a court remembered for war and recovery, a Jain merchant-minister chose marble over menace. His Vimal Vasahi shows how patronage can turn the brief weight of power into beauty that outlives fear.
